account: DARPA's results release describes the Final Competition. Teams' cyber reasoning systems tried to find and patch synthetic vulnerabilities across 54 million lines of real-world open-source code. They found 54 unique synthetic vulnerabilities in 63 challenges and patched 43. They also found 18 real, non-synthetic vulnerabilities (six in C codebases, 12 in Java). DARPA said that these were being responsibly disclosed. There were 11 patches for real bugs. The average cost was about $152 per task. Team Atlanta (Georgia Tech, Samsung Research, KAIST, POSTECH) won $4 million, Trail of Bits $3 million and Theori $1.5 million. Four of seven systems were released open source. The Record reported the same figures from Las Vegas with program manager Andrew Carney's remarks. On 22 October 2025 curl maintainer Daniel Stenberg, whose project was among the targets, examined the injected curl flaws. He judged that they were straightforward and not deeply hidden. In March 2026 Team Atlanta reported that the released systems were hard to run outside their teams. It also reported that a ported Atlantis found 10 new bugs, three of high severity, in eight OSS-Fuzz projects. In September 2026 researchers at the University of Maryland tested the top three AIxCC systems on 213 transplanted vulnerabilities. Across 11 agents, they found that checks based only on the original crash input overstate patching success by 1.83 times on average. Atlantis passed 92.0% of the original crash checks and solved 48.4% of tasks under full validation. The researchers also found that the AIxCC systems solved fewer tasks than general-purpose coding agents on the same model.

ai_role.statement: DARPA, the organizer, reports the figures. The Record corroborates from the event. Stenberg's independent look at the curl tasks suggests the injected flaws were easy. That bounds how much the synthetic scores show.

fields.account: DARPA's results release describes the Final Competition. Teams' cyber reasoning systems tried to find and patch synthetic vulnerabilities across 54 million lines of real-world open-source code. They found 54 unique synthetic vulnerabilities in 63 challenges and patched 43. They also found 18 real, non-synthetic vulnerabilities (six in C codebases, 12 in Java). DARPA said that these were being responsibly disclosed. There were 11 patches for real bugs. The average cost was about $152 per task. Team Atlanta (Georgia Tech, Samsung Research, KAIST, POSTECH) won $4 million, Trail of Bits $3 million and Theori $1.5 million. Four of seven systems were released open source. The Record reported the same figures from Las Vegas with program manager Andrew Carney's remarks. On 22 October 2025 curl maintainer Daniel Stenberg, whose project was among the targets, examined the injected curl flaws. He judged that they were straightforward and not deeply hidden. In March 2026 Team Atlanta reported that the released systems were hard to run outside their teams. It also reported that a ported Atlantis found 10 new bugs, three of high severity, in eight OSS-Fuzz projects. In September 2026 researchers at the University of Maryland tested the top three AIxCC systems on 213 transplanted vulnerabilities. Across 11 agents, they found that checks based only on the original crash input overstate patching success by 1.83 times on average. Atlantis passed 92.0% of the original crash checks and solved 48.4% of tasks under full validation. The researchers also found that the AIxCC systems solved fewer tasks than general-purpose coding agents on the same model.
